warnings: Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: Clarify earlier that the lesson implements a causal trailing moving average, distinguishing it from a centered moving average that would require future samples and is unsuitable for real-time control.
The lesson is exceptionally complete but somewhat long for a foundational class. The repeated explanations of spike influence, delay, and startup behavior could be consolidated to improve pacing.
Add one compact expected-results table for window sizes 1, 3, and 5, so students can compare smoothing and responsiveness without relying only on visual inspection.
The phrase 'three nearby measurements' could briefly note that the measurements are separated in time, not simultaneous readings from three sensors.

The Python lab is well aligned, but an optional efficient implementation using a fixed-size buffer and running sum would better connect the lesson to memory and computation constraints mentioned in the real-robot section.

The 'See It in Your Head' section contains both an existing schematic and instructions describing what an illustrator could show. Remove or revise the latter so the section reads as intentional lesson content rather than leftover asset direction.
Add a direct safety note in the lab telling students not to connect the example to motors or collision-avoidance hardware without testing latency and emergency-stop behavior.
The lesson could explicitly state that a moving average attenuates some high-frequency variation but does not necessarily remove periodic noise, bias, dropouts, or correlated errors.
The generated visuals are relevant and well captioned, but a real photograph of a rover and distance sensor would materially strengthen the physical-hardware connection.
